problem: Every component covered so far — CPU, RAM, Storage, Motherboard — is an electrical device that does absolutely nothing without stable, correctly-regulated electricity. Wall power (AC, 110V/220V, fluctuating) is completely incompatible with what sensitive electronics need (clean, stable, low-voltage DC). Worse, in the real world, power fails: outages, brownouts, surges. A business running a database server cannot simply accept 'the power went out, so the server crashed and possibly corrupted data' as a normal cost of doing business. The industry needed both a way to convert and regulate power for components, and a way to keep systems running (or shut down gracefully) when input power fails.
concept: Power, in infrastructure terms, covers two related things: the Power Supply Unit (PSU) that converts wall AC power into the stable DC voltages each component needs, and power redundancy/continuity systems (UPS, generators, redundant power supplies) that keep systems running or allow graceful shutdown when input power is disrupted.
deep: ● PSU function: Converts AC (alternating current, from the wall) to DC (direct current) at specific voltages (commonly +12V, +5V, +3.3V rails) that the motherboard, CPU, storage, and other components require.
Different components draw different amounts of current at different voltages.

● Wattage and headroom: A PSU is rated for maximum wattage it can deliver. Enterprise builds intentionally provision headroom above calculated draw — running a PSU near its maximum rating continuously reduces its lifespan and efficiency.

● Efficiency ratings (80 PLUS Bronze/Gold/Platinum/Titanium): Measures how much input AC power is converted to usable DC power vs wasted as heat. Higher efficiency matters enormously at data-center scale, where wasted watts translate directly into cooling costs and electricity bills across thousands of servers.

● Redundant PSUs: Enterprise servers commonly ship with two (or more) power supplies, each capable of powering the entire server alone. If one fails or loses input power (e.g., one is plugged into a failed circuit), the other keeps the server running with zero downtime — this is a hardware-level high-availability feature, previewed here and formalized in Layer 5's HA session.

● UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply): A battery-backed device sitting between wall power and the server, providing near-instant power during an outage — long enough either to ride out a brief blip or to allow a graceful, controlled shutdown before battery depletes.

● Generators: For longer outages, data centers use diesel or gas generators that can sustain operations for hours to days, with UPS batteries bridging the gap during the generator's startup time (typically 10-30 seconds).

● PDU (Power Distribution Unit): Rack-mounted device distributing power from the data center's electrical infrastructure to individual servers, often with per-outlet monitoring and remote power-cycling capability.
workflow: Wall/data-center AC power | UPS (battery-backed, filters/conditions power) | PDU (distributes power within the rack) | Server PSU (converts AC -> regulated DC, often dual/redundant) | DC power delivered to motherboard, CPU, RAM, storage | If input power fails:
UPS battery sustains load -> generator starts (if present) -> UPS hands off to generator -> or graceful OS shutdown triggered
enterprise: Power infrastructure exists at multiple layers in an enterprise: redundant PSUs inside each server, rack-level PDUs (often dual, fed from separate electrical circuits/utility feeds for true redundancy), UPS systems for the data center or server room, and often backup generators for larger facilities. Even a modest 500-employee company's server room typically has at minimum a rack UPS; larger enterprises design entire electrical topology (dual utility feeds, N+1 or 2N redundancy) as a core part of Layer 5 (High Availability / Disaster Recovery).
dependencies: ● Utility electrical supply (or on-site generation) ● Physical wiring and circuit capacity of the building/data center ● UPS battery health (batteries degrade over time and need testing/replacement)
dependents: Literally everything depends on power — CPU, RAM, storage, motherboard, networking equipment, cooling systems. Power is the most foundational dependency in the entire Knowledge Map; every layer above Layer 1 ultimately traces back to a stable power source.
security: ● Attacks: Power-based denial of service (physically cutting power, or in rare documented cases, malware designed to manipulate power draw/thermal behavior to damage hardware); social engineering to gain physical access to power infrastructure.

● Mistakes: No UPS or generator testing schedule (batteries silently fail and are only discovered dead during an actual outage), single points of failure in power feeds (both PSUs plugged into the same circuit, defeating redundancy), no documented graceful-shutdown automation tied to UPS status.

● Best practices: Regularly test UPS battery health and failover, ensure redundant PSUs are fed from genuinely separate circuits/panels, automate graceful shutdown scripts triggered by UPS software when battery runs low, physically secure power infrastructure (locked server rooms/racks).

● Detection: Unexpected power events (unplanned reboots across multiple servers simultaneously) should trigger investigation — this pattern often distinguishes a power incident from a targeted attack on a single system.
troubleshooting: ● Symptom: Server randomly reboots under heavy load but not idle. Root cause: PSU insufficient wattage/aging PSU unable to sustain peak draw, distinct from a CPU/motherboard fault (Session 4).
● Symptom: Both redundant PSUs show as failed simultaneously. Root cause: often not two coincidental hardware failures, but a shared upstream circuit/PDU failure — a classic 'false redundancy' trap.
● Symptom: UPS alarms during a brief power blip that shouldn't have mattered. Root cause: degraded/end- of-life UPS battery no longer holding sufficient charge.

● Diagnosis approach: Check PSU status LEDs/management interface first → verify both redundant feeds are actually on separate upstream circuits → check UPS battery health/self-test logs → correlate reboot timing across multiple servers to distinguish a power event from an isolated hardware fault.
example: A company's server room loses utility power during a storm. The UPS carries the load for the expected few minutes while the generator starts — but the generator fails to start due to a stale fuel issue from lack of testing. The UPS batteries deplete before power is restored, causing an unclean shutdown of several servers, including a database server that suffers minor data corruption on an in-progress write. The post-incident review finds the generator hadn't been load-tested in over a year — a direct, avoidable process failure, not a technology failure.
cloud: Cloud providers operate power infrastructure at a scale and redundancy level (multiple utility feeds, on-site generation, massive UPS/battery systems, often across multiple physically separate 'Availability Zones') that is effectively impossible for most individual companies to replicate. This is one of the strongest practical arguments for cloud adoption: power reliability engineering becomes the provider's problem, not yours — though you still must design your application to handle an entire Availability Zone going down, which is a software/architecture responsibility, not a hardware one.
automation: ● PowerShell: Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery for UPS/battery status where supported; vendor-specific PowerShell modules (e.g., APC PowerChute) automate graceful shutdown on UPS events.
● Bash: apcupsd or nut (Network UPS Tools) daemons on Linux monitor UPS status and trigger scripted shutdowns.
● Enterprise tooling: Out-of-band management (iDRAC/iLO, from Session 4) typically exposes PSU status and power draw metrics via API/SNMP for centralized monitoring dashboards.
career: ● SysAdmin: Monitoring PSU/UPS health, configuring graceful automated shutdown scripts, coordinating with facilities on power redundancy design.
● Blue Team: Correlating unexpected power events with security incidents; understanding physical security's role in protecting power infrastructure.
● DevSecOps: Rarely hands-on with physical power, but should design applications assuming any single power domain can fail (informs cloud multi-AZ architecture decisions).
● Cloud Security Engineer: Understanding provider SLAs around power/availability zones, and designing for graceful degradation when an AZ experiences an outage.
interview: ● Beginner: What does a power supply unit (PSU) actually do?
● Intermediate: Why do enterprise servers typically have two power supplies, and what could defeat that redundancy?
● Senior: Walk through what should happen, end to end, when a data center loses utility power.
● Architect: How would you design power redundancy (feeds, PDUs, UPS, generator) for a new data center build to eliminate single points of failure?
misconceptions: ● "Redundant power supplies mean the server can never lose power." Only true if the two supplies are actually fed from independent circuits — a very common misconfiguration defeats this.

● "A UPS is meant to run a server indefinitely during an outage." Most UPS systems are designed to bridge a short gap or enable graceful shutdown, not to sustain long-term operation — that's the generator's job.
● "Cloud means I never have to think about power." You don't manage physical power, but you still must architect for an entire Availability Zone failing.
anchors: Power is the electricity flowing into the kitchen itself — without it, the fridge (RAM), the stove (CPU), and the pantry lighting (storage access) simply don't function, no matter how well-designed the kitchen (motherboard) is. A UPS is like a generator-powered flashlight you grab the instant the lights flicker — enough to finish plating the current dish safely, not to cook a full dinner.
connections: Power is what the motherboard (Session 4) distributes to the CPU, RAM, and storage (Sessions 1-3) — it's the literal foundation beneath every other hardware session. It directly sets up Session 9 (Hardware Troubleshooting) and previews concepts formalized later in Layer 5 (High Availability, Disaster Recovery) and Layer 9 (Cloud Availability Zones).

lab: ● Research your own laptop's power adapter: find its rated wattage output and compare it to your CPU's TDP (Thermal Design Power) spec — this shows the relationship between component draw and PSU sizing at a small scale.
● On your Windows Server 2019 VM (or physical Windows machine): run Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery to see what battery/power info Windows exposes.
● If you have access to any UPS (even a small consumer one), find its runtime rating at a given load and calculate how long it would sustain a specific server's estimated power draw.
● Research: look up your FundedNext-relevant server room or hosting provider's stated power redundancy (N+1, 2N) if publicly documented, to connect this concept to your real work environment.
